transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it’s good to meet you too, Doc, though I’ll be honest, I wouldn’t be here if it weren’t for my family and some folks at work making a big fuss. They all keep telling me I’m doing too much, going too fast, taking on more than a man my age should. I’m 74, sure, but I’ve got more energy now than I did twenty years ago. It’s like, to me, it feels like I’m the only one with enough drive to actually get things done. We’re in the middle of this big move, you see, and there’s a million details. The boxes, the packing, the logistics—nobody else was stepping up, so I took charge. And then there’s the new house. The garage there is an absolute disaster, structurally unsound, poorly designed. So I’ve been drawing up the blueprints to rebuild it right, you know, from the ground up. I’ve been up most nights working on the plans. 

And that’s not even half of it. Down at the church, things were getting sloppy with the charity drives, so I’ve been organizing all of that, making sure the schedules are tight and the volunteers know what they’re doing. Plus, I’m still working full time at the plant—crushing and blending, heavy industrial stuff. These younger fellows they hire nowadays, they don't know the first thing about how the machines actually work or the right way to mix the materials to get the proper yield. I have to show them, step by step, how the job ought to be done. If I don't do it, the whole line slows down. So, I’m handling the move, the garage, the church, and the young guys at work, and everyone’s telling me to slow down. But if I slow down, who’s going to do it all? It just doesn't make any sense to me why they're so worried when I'm finally getting everything accomplished.
Have you been needing less sleep than usual?

Needing less sleep? Well, I don't know if I'd say I *need* less, or if I've even noticed a real change in what my body requires... I haven't really been paying attention to the clock like that. I mean, what does "need" even mean, really? You sleep when you're tired, and right now, I'm just not tired. 

Like I was saying, I've been up most nights with those blueprints for the garage, and let me tell you, when you're in the zone, when you're really figuring out the load-bearing requirements for a proper roof truss system, time just flies. My wife, she goes to bed around nine, always has, regular as a metronome. But me? I'll sit there at the kitchen table with my drafting pencils—the good wooden ones, not that cheap plastic stuff they sell at the hardware store nowadays—and I'll get to sketching. The next thing I know, the sun is coming up over the neighbor's roof. 

And I feel fantastic! I don't feel groggy, I don't need a whole pot of coffee to get going. I just head right out to the driveway in the morning light to measure out the pour for the new concrete foundation before I have to head into the plant for my shift. Back in my thirties, I used to work double shifts at the crusher and I'd be dead on my feet by Friday, but this is completely different. So, I don't know if I'm technically needing less sleep, I'm not really sure about the science of it all. I just know that lying in bed with my eyes closed feels like a complete and utter waste of time when I have all this energy and a whole list of critical tasks that absolutely will not get done if I don't do them.
Have you been having trouble with your memory lately?

Memory? No, no, my memory is sharp as a tack. Sharper, even. I don't know why everyone keeps asking me about my memory lately, like I'm some doddering old fool who can't remember where he left his spectacles. Just the other day, my daughter—she's the one who really pushed for this whole appointment, bless her heart, she means well but she worries too much—she asked me if I remembered to call the moving company to confirm the truck size. And I told her, I didn't just remember to call them, I remembered the exact cubic footage we need based on my own calculations of the living room furniture, which, by the way, I had to measure twice because the first time I didn't account for the slant in the back of the sofa. 

I remember everything right now. It's like my brain is firing on all cylinders. I can recall the exact mix ratio for the industrial blender at the plant—the one we used back in '85 before they switched to the automated system that doesn't even get the consistency right. I can tell you the names of all the volunteers on the Tuesday morning church roster, and I can even tell you who was late last week. Mrs. Higgins, five minutes late, blamed it on traffic, but I know she just stops for coffee. 

So, no, trouble with my memory? Absolutely not. If anything, I'm remembering things I hadn't thought about in years, and I'm connecting the dots faster than anyone else around me. It's everyone else who seems to be forgetting things, like forgetting how to do their jobs properly or forgetting that I've got this whole move completely under control. I don't need a notepad, I don't need reminders on my phone—which I still say is too small to type on anyway—I just keep it all right up here, and it's clearer than it's ever been.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people don’t seem to hear or see?

Hearing or seeing things? Like... hallucinations? No, no, I haven't got anything like that going on. I know my mind is racing a mile a minute, but my eyes and ears are working exactly the same as they always have. 

Well, I mean, I see things other people don't see, but not in the way you mean. Not ghosts or visions or anything crazy like that. I see things because I'm actually paying attention. Like down at the plant, I can see the exact moment the mixture starts to clump in the hopper—the younger guys, they just stare at their phones, but I can see the texture changing, I can hear the pitch of the motor whining just a fraction of a decibel higher when the load gets too heavy. That's just experience, you know? Forty years on the line, you learn to see and hear the machinery like it's a living thing. 

And with the new house, too. I walked into that garage and I saw the problem immediately. The previous owner, whoever he was, he tried to shore up the center beam with a couple of two-by-fours that weren't even pressure-treated. I saw the bowing in the wood before I even took a tape measure to it. My son-in-law, he walked right in there and said it looked fine to him. Fine! I told him, "You're looking at it, but you're not seeing it." 

So, no, my senses are perfectly grounded in reality. In fact, I'd argue I'm seeing reality a lot clearer than most folks these days. People walk around with blinders on, missing all the details, missing the big picture, and then they wonder why things fall apart. But me? I'm catching everything. I see the structural flaws, I hear the engine strain, I notice when the church bulletin has a typo in the second paragraph. But as for hearing voices or seeing things that aren't physically there? Absolutely not. My mind is sharp, Doc, it's not playing tricks on me. It's just working better than everyone else's right now.
Is this burst of energy and activity a clear change from how you’re usually like?

A change? Well, I suppose you could call it a change, but I prefer to think of it as an awakening, really. You see, for the last few years, especially since I hit my seventies, people just expect you to slow down. They expect you to sit in a recliner and watch the golf channel and let the world pass you by. And maybe I was doing a bit of that. Maybe I was coming home from the plant, having my dinner, and just nodding off in front of the television. My wife would say, "Frank, you're always tired," and I'd say, "I've been mixing concrete and crushing aggregate for four decades, of course I'm tired." 

But this? This is entirely different. It's not just a change, it's a complete reversal! I feel like I did back in 1982 when we got the contract for the new municipal building and I was working sixty-hour weeks and still had the energy to build that deck on the back of our first house on Elm Street. I mean, I haven't felt this kind of drive, this absolute compulsion to get things done, in years. Decades, maybe! 

Just look at what I've accomplished in the last three weeks alone. I've completely redesigned the garage, I've reorganized the entire tool shed—and let me tell you, finding a proper sorting system for three generations of drill bits is no small feat—and I've been pulling my full shifts at the plant without breaking a sweat. The younger guys, they look at me like I've grown a second head. They're dragging their feet by 3 PM, and I'm practically jogging across the factory floor to check the hopper levels. 

So, yes, it's a change from how I've been recently, but it's a change for the better! It's like someone flipped a switch in my brain and suddenly all the fog is gone, all the fatigue is gone, and I'm finally operating at maximum capacity again. My daughter says it's "concerning," but what's concerning about a man finally getting his projects done? What's concerning about waking up with a sense of purpose instead of just waiting around to get old? I'll tell you what, Doc, if this is a change, I don't ever want to change back.
Before this burst of energy started, was there a time when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed? No, no, I wouldn't use a word like that. People throw that word around entirely too much these days, if you ask me. Everyone's always talking about being depressed if they have a bad Tuesday, you know? But no, I wasn't sad or... or moping around feeling sorry for myself. 

Like I was just saying, I was tired. But there is a world of difference between being tired from working a physically demanding job and being depressed. You try standing on concrete floors for eight hours a day at my age, making sure the aggregate is ground to the exact right specification—because let me tell you, if the moisture content is off by even a fraction of a percent, the whole batch is ruined and the foreman is breathing down your neck. That takes a toll on a man! It takes a toll on the knees, on the lower back. 

So, sure, I'd come home, eat my meatloaf or whatever the wife made, and I'd sit in my recliner. I'd watch the evening news, maybe doze off right in the middle of the local weather report. My wife, she'd say I was in a rut. "Frank," she'd say, "you never want to go out anymore, you don't want to go to the diner on Friday nights like we used to." But that's not depression! That's just... resting. I had earned the right to sit in my chair. 

I never felt down in the dumps. I got up every single morning at 4:30 AM, just like I have since 1978, I made my coffee—black, none of that flavored nonsense they sell now—and I went to work and did my job. A depressed man doesn't do that. A depressed man can't even get out of bed, or so I hear on those commercials they play during the golf tournaments. You know the ones, with the little cartoon clouds following people around? I didn't have any clouds following me. I just had a bit of fatigue. Which, as I’ve been telling you, is completely gone now anyway! Completely vanished. So no, no depression at all. Just a long, well-earned rest before this second wind finally kicked in.
Before this burst of energy started, did you have any recent illness, stroke, head injury, or other new medical problem?

Illness? A stroke? Ha! No, no, absolutely not. Do I look like a man who just had a stroke? I mean, really, look at me. My hands are steady as a rock—watch this, not a tremor, not a shake. You don't spend forty years wrestling with heavy machinery and industrial mixers if you've got a weak constitution. No, my health is perfect. Better than perfect, honestly. I haven't even had so much as a cold, a sniffle, or a sore throat in... well, I can't even remember the last time I took a sick day at the plant. Maybe back in '98 when that terrible flu went around, and even then, I only stayed home because the wife practically locked the front door on me. 

As for a head injury? Not a chance. I wear my hard hat every single day on the floor. It's a strict regulation, sure, but it's also just common sense. You get these young kids coming in, they want to take their helmets off the second the foreman turns his back because they're sweating or it messes up their hair. I tell them, "You want a cracked skull when a piece of aggregate flies off the belt? Be my guest." But me? I follow the protocols. I'm aware of my surroundings. I haven't bumped my head on so much as a kitchen cabinet. 

So no, no strokes, no head injuries, no mysterious new medical problems. I've always been told I've got the constitution of a man twenty years younger anyway. It's the physical labor, you see. It keeps the blood pumping. People sit at these desks all day, staring at screens, and their bodies just atrophy. They turn to mush. Then they get to my age and they're falling apart, having strokes, breaking hips, taking a dozen pills with their breakfast. But I'm on my feet, I'm moving, I'm lifting. 

You can completely cross any of that medical stuff off your list, Doc. This energy isn't some side effect of being sick or hitting my head. Like I said, it's the exact opposite of being sick. It's just me, finally firing on all cylinders and getting things done the way they're supposed to be done!
Have you ever had another time in your life when you felt unusually energized and driven like this?

Another time? Well, let me think about that. I mean, like I mentioned a minute ago, I've always been a hard worker. You don't survive in the industrial mixing business if you're lazy, that's for sure. I've had periods where I had to put my nose to the grindstone, absolutely. 

Take 1976, for instance. That was the year my son was born. I was working my regular shifts at the plant, of course, but I also picked up a paper route in the early mornings—had to be up at 3 AM for that, driving all over the county in this beat-up old Ford—and on weekends I was doing landscaping for the Johnsons down the street. Nice people, the Johnsons. They ended up moving to Boca Raton back in '94, I think it was, or maybe '95. Anyway, I was working essentially three jobs to save up for a better house for the family. So I was driven, sure. I had a goal, I had ambition. 

But was I energized like this? No. Absolutely not. Back then, I was running on sheer willpower and maybe a little too much cheap diner coffee. I was dragging myself out of bed every morning. I'd get home and my work boots would feel like they were made of solid lead. I was productive, but I was exhausted. 

This thing happening right now, this... this absolute surge? It's completely unprecedented. I have never felt anything even close to this in my entire seventy-four years on this earth. Even when I was eighteen and thought I could conquer the world, I still needed to sleep! I still got tired after a long day of hauling materials. But now? I don't feel the fatigue. I don't feel the drag. It's like my body just bypassed the need for all that. 

So, no, Doc, I can confidently say I have never, ever experienced a time like this before. Never. This is a brand new chapter, and let me tell you, it's the best one yet. I mean, if I had felt like this in my thirties, I would own the plant by now! I would be running the whole tri-state operation! I wouldn't just be checking the hoppers, I'd be designing the whole manufacturing line! It's just a shame it took until I was in my seventies to finally unlock all this potential, you know?
Have you started any new medications or substances recently?

New medications? Ha! No, no, absolutely not. I don't believe in taking a pill for every little thing, never have. You go to some of these doctors—and no offense to you, Doc, I know you're just doing your job here—but you go to a clinic these days and they want to put you on a pill to wake up, a pill to go to sleep, a pill to digest your meatloaf... it's a racket! I haven't started any new medications because I don't even take any old ones. Like I said, my health is perfect. Better than perfect. 

And substances? If you mean drugs or... or whatever, well, I should hope you know better than to ask a man like me that. I've been working at the same plant since Jimmy Carter was in office! We get drug tested randomly, you know. Strict OSHA regulations. Safety first, always. You absolutely cannot be operating a three-ton industrial mixer, calibrating the aggregate flow, if you're hopped up on... whatever it is the kids are taking these days. You'd lose an arm, or worse, you'd ruin a fifty-thousand-dollar batch of concrete! 

And even the legal stuff, the over-the-counter junk? I don't touch it. I see these young guys on the floor, they come in at 6 AM for the early shift clutching these giant cans of energy drinks. Neon green cans, looks like actual antifreeze, smells like bubblegum and battery acid. They chug those things just to keep their eyes open! It's pathetic, really. I tell them, "You're rotting your stomach lining! You're gonna have an ulcer by the time you're thirty!" But they don't listen. Me? I drink my black coffee at 4:30 in the morning, made in my regular drip pot, and that is it. I don't need pills, I don't need powders, I don't need vitamins, and I certainly don't need neon energy drinks. 

So no, I haven't started taking anything at all. Nothing. This energy you're seeing right now? This drive to just get up and conquer the day? It's one hundred percent pure, unadulterated Frank. Just natural, God-given vitality that's finally been completely unleashed. Why in the world would I mess a good thing up by putting chemicals in my body?
Have you done anything lately that got you into trouble or worried your family, like spending money unusually, making risky decisions, or acting out of character?

Trouble? Worried? Well, if you ask Martha—that's my wife—she’s always worried. That’s just her nature, she could find a reason to worry about a sunny day. But "trouble"? I wouldn't call it trouble. I'd call it taking initiative, which apparently scares people who are used to moving at a snail's pace. 

I mean, look, I did go ahead and put some deposits down on some major garage work and a whole bunch of new equipment. Top-of-the-line stuff, too. A commercial-grade air compressor, a heavy-duty hydraulic lift, new welding gear. I realized our garage was completely underutilized, just sitting there holding boxes of old Christmas decorations when it could be a fully operational workshop! And, alright, no, I didn't exactly talk it over with Martha before writing the checks. But you have to understand, if I bring it up to her, she wants to sit down, look at the budget, think about it for three weeks, and by then the opportunity is gone! I had the vision, I had the energy, so I pulled the trigger. She hit the roof, of course. Started going on and on about the savings account, but I told her, you have to invest to build something great! 

And I've just been so busy with it all. I kept driving back and forth, back and forth between the houses—our main place and that old rental property of ours across town—just trying to get everything measured and prepped at both locations simultaneously. I mean, I was making that drive four, maybe five times a day, just boom, boom, boom, getting it done. Martha said I was driving like a maniac, but my reflexes are sharper than they've been in decades! 

It’s the same story at the plant, honestly. People get so stuck in their little routines. I started rushing some of the mixing jobs on the floor because I realized we were wasting so much time on these redundant safety checks that I can do in my sleep. I know the exact second that aggregate is perfectly blended, I don't need a timer to tell me! But the foreman, Dave—and a couple of the other guys, actually—they pulled me aside and got all bent out of shape. They warned me I was taking chances. Taking chances! Can you believe that? I've been running those hoppers since before Dave even had a driver's license, and he's telling me I'm taking chances just because I'm finally working at maximum efficiency. 

So, sure, maybe they're all a little "worried" or whatever you want to call it. But that's just because they can't keep up with me right now!
Do you believe you have special abilities or powers that other people do not have?

Special abilities or powers? Like... like what, like Superman? Ha! No, no, Doc, I’m not sitting here thinking I can fly off the roof or bend steel beams with my bare hands, if that’s what you’re getting at. I know the difference between comic books and reality. I used to read all those superhero comics to my son back when he was a little guy in the early eighties—Spider-Man, Captain America, all of that. So no, I don't have magic powers. 

But if you’re asking if I have abilities that other people don’t have? Well, if you want to call forty-five years of hands-on, hard-earned experience an "ability," then absolutely I do. I mean, I can walk onto the floor at the plant, close my eyes, and just listen to the hum of a three-ton industrial mixer, and I can tell you exactly what the moisture content of that batch is. I can hear if the aggregate is too coarse. I can feel the vibration in the floor grates and know if the secondary valve is sticking. 

Is that a superpower? No! It’s just knowing your craft! But you look at these kids they hire today, these guys fresh out of some technical program, and they need a computer screen to tell them the mix is off. They need digital sensors and flashing red alarms. Me? I just know. And right now, with this... this incredible energy I have, my mind is just processing all of that information so much faster. It's instantaneous. 

Like just the other day, Dave—the foreman I was telling you about—he was staring at his little tablet, scratching his head because the viscosity numbers were dropping on hopper number three. I just walked right past him, didn't even look at his screen, and I said, "Dave, your water line pressure is too high, you're washing out the cement." He looked at me like I had two heads! He didn't believe me, wanted to run a full diagnostic. Took him twenty minutes to shut the line down and check, and what do you know? Pressure regulator was shot. 

So people see me doing that, they see me moving this fast and anticipating problems before the computers even register them, and I guess they don't know what to make of it. They think it's unnatural because they're all moving in slow motion! But it's not a superpower. It's just absolute, crystal-clear focus. It’s my brain finally firing on all cylinders, without any of the rust or the fatigue holding me back. So no, no magic powers here, Doc. Just Frank, operating at peak efficiency.
Have you recently been told you have a thyroid problem?

Thyroid? A thyroid problem? Ha! No, no, absolutely not. I don't have any gland issues. You know, it's funny you ask that, because Martha's sister, Susan, she had a thyroid thing back in... oh, it must have been the late nineties. Or maybe early two-thousands? Anyway, she was always sluggish, sitting on the sofa all day, complaining about being cold, watching her daytime stories. They told her it was her thyroid and put her on some pill she has to take for the rest of her natural life. But me? Look at me! I am the exact opposite of sluggish. 

I go in for my physical—well, I haven't been in a couple of years because, like I said, I don't need to go looking for trouble when I feel this good—but the last time I went, Dr. Miller did that thing where they stand behind you and press on your throat and tell you to swallow. You know what I'm talking about? He did that, and he said everything was perfectly normal. Perfect size, perfect whatever it is they feel for in there. 

I know why you're asking, though. I'm not stupid. You're looking at me, you're seeing all this drive, this... this absolute fire I have right now, and you're thinking, "Oh, it must be a hyper-active thyroid, his metabolism is out of whack, his glands are working overtime." But I'm telling you, it's not a medical condition! It's not a gland acting up. It's just me! 

Why is it so hard for people to believe that a man my age can just wake up and feel fantastic? I've got the stamina of a guy half my age, and I didn't need a wonky thyroid to get it. No thyroid problems, no heart problems, no nothing. Just pure, natural energy. So, no, nobody has told me I have a thyroid problem, because my thyroid is doing exactly what it's supposed to do.
Have you had any recent medical tests that showed something abnormal?

Medical tests? Abnormal? No, listen to me, Doc, I haven't had any tests done because I haven't needed any tests done! Why would I go sit in some freezing cold waiting room, reading a three-year-old copy of Field & Stream, just to have somebody poke me with a needle and tell me what I already know? 

I mean, think about it. You take your truck to the mechanic when it's making a funny noise, right? When the transmission slips or the radiator is blowing steam. You don't take it in when it's purring like a kitten and hauling a full payload without breaking a sweat! And that's me right now. I am a finely tuned engine. 

Martha, of course, she’s always on me about it. "Frank, you need your cholesterol checked, Frank, you need your prostate checked." It’s always something with her. I think it was last year—or maybe it was the year before, right around Thanksgiving because I remember we were setting up the deep fryer for the turkey out on the driveway—she was nagging me to go get a full blood workup just because I hit my seventies. She gets these ideas in her head from watching those morning shows, you know? They have some doctor on there in a nice suit talking about vitamin deficiencies and suddenly she thinks I need twelve vials of blood drawn. But I told her, I said, "Martha, they're not going to find anything abnormal except maybe that I've got the blood pressure of a college athlete!" 

So no, no recent tests, no abnormal results. I steer clear of all those machines and monitors and clipboards unless something is actually broken, and right now, let me tell you, every single part of me is working better than it ever has. If they hooked me up to one of those EKG machines right now, it would probably just print out a gold star! So no, nothing abnormal, no tests at all.
Have there been times recently when you felt confused about where you were or what day it was?

Confused? Me? Ha! Doc, you've got to be kidding. I haven't been confused a day in my life, and certainly not lately! If anything, I'm the only one around here who actually knows what day it is, what time it is, and what exactly is supposed to be happening at any given second! 

Just... just the other morning, Martha—she comes into the kitchen, rubbing her eyes, hair all a mess, and she says, "Frank, what are you doing up, it's Sunday." Sunday! I looked at her, I already had my work boots laced up, coffee in hand, the newspaper read cover to cover, and I said, "Martha, it is Tuesday the 14th, it's 3:45 in the morning, the recycling goes out today—which I already took down to the curb, by the way—and I have to be at the plant because the new shipment of medium-grade silica sand is arriving on truck number four at exactly 4:30." 

And you know what? I drove down to the yard, and who was pulling in right as I parked? Truck number four. Exactly on schedule. 

So no, I don't get confused about where I am or what day it is. It's everyone else who's walking around in a fog! You look at Dave, the foreman I mentioned earlier. Last Wednesday—or, wait, no, it was Thursday, because they were serving that terrible meatloaf in the cafeteria and they only do that on Thursdays—Dave scheduled the routine maintenance on the primary crusher for the middle of the first shift! Who does that? He got his days mixed up, thought it was a weekend! He's half my age and he's the one who doesn't know what day of the week it is. 

But my mind? It's like a steel trap right now, Doc. A steel trap! I can tell you what day it is, what the date is, what the weather was doing this time last year. Everything is just filed away perfectly in my head and I can pull it up the second I need it. I don't need a calendar, I don't need a watch. I just feel the rhythm of the week. So no, no confusion here. None at all. I know exactly where I am, exactly why I'm here, and exactly what's going on around me.
Has a doctor who examined you recently told you that you have any new medical illness?

New medical illness? Doc, I feel like we're going in circles here! I really do. Like I was just saying about the tests—you have to actually go to a doctor for them to tell you that you have an illness! And why would I go? I work at the plant, right? I'm running the heavy mixers, the industrial grinders, the whole nine yards. You think a guy with a "new medical illness" can stand on his feet for fourteen hours straight on a concrete floor, managing the silica and the aggregate? Not a chance. 

You know how it is, you go into one of those offices, and they just want to find something wrong so they can put a label on you and bill your insurance. My buddy Ron—he operates the secondary crusher down at the yard—he went in for a simple cough, just a little tickle in his throat from the plant dust, and they told him he had some kind of new respiratory thing and gave him three different inhalers! Three! I told him, "Ron, you're breathing in pulverized granite all day, of course you're coughing, you don't need a plastic tube to fix that!" 

But me? No, no one has told me a thing because I don't give them the chance to go fishing for problems that don't exist. I don't have a single symptom of anything. I am the absolute picture of health. A new illness... ha! I'm practically Benjamin Button over here, getting younger and stronger every single day! So no, no new illnesses, no old illnesses, no illnesses at all.
Have you had any recent blood tests or a brain scan?

Blood tests? A brain scan? Doc, are you even listening to me? I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here, I really do. I just told you, I haven't been to a doctor! I haven't had any tests! Why on earth would I need a brain scan? 

Do I look like a guy who needs his head examined by some giant, clanking magnetic tube? I know all about those MRI machines, you know. My sister-in-law, Brenda, she had to get one a few years back for her neck, and she said they slide you in there like a loaf of bread into an oven, and it sounds like somebody is in there with a jackhammer for forty-five minutes straight. A jackhammer! I already listen to industrial crushers and heavy-duty grinders all day long down at the plant. I've got the sweet symphony of pulverized rock and roaring diesel engines in my ears from sunup to sundown. Why would I volunteer to lay in a plastic tube and listen to more noise just so some technician can look at a picture of my brain? 

And blood tests, again with the blood tests! I already told you about Martha nagging me about that. No, I haven't had any blood tests. Nobody has drawn my blood, nobody has scanned my brain, nobody has hooked me up to any wires or monitors or anything else. My brain is working at maximum capacity right now. A hundred and ten percent! If they scanned my brain, the machine would probably short out from all the electricity firing up there! It's like a supercomputer, Doc, processing a million things a second. I don't need a scan to tell me that. So no, no blood tests, no brain scans, no nothing. I'm telling you, I am in the absolute prime of my life right now!
Before this started, did you recently have any surgery or medical procedure?

Surgery? Doc, I... I just don't know how else to say this. I feel like I'm speaking a different language here! No, no surgeries. No medical procedures. No doctors in scrubs coming at me with scalpels or lasers or whatever else they use these days. 

Before this started? Before what started? Me feeling fantastic? Me finally having the energy to get things done at the plant the way they're supposed to be done? Because let me tell you, if feeling this good requires a surgery, everybody would be lining up for it! But no, I haven't been near a hospital. I haven't been near an operating room. 

The last time I had anything even close to a procedure was... oh, gosh, it must have been nineteen ninety-eight. Maybe ninety-nine? No, ninety-eight, because it was the year my son graduated high school and we had that big party in the backyard, and I couldn't even eat the ribs we grilled because I had just gotten a root canal. A root canal! That's the closest I've come to a medical procedure in decades, and even that was just a dentist with a drill, not a real surgery. 

And you know, even then, I bounced right back. I was back at the plant the next day, jaw swollen out to here, looking like a chipmunk hoarding walnuts, but I was running the industrial mixers just fine. I don't stop, Doc. I don't have time to lay up in some hospital bed recovering from a surgery. Who would make sure the aggregate is blended right? Dave? Ha! We already established Dave doesn't even know what day it is! If I took two weeks off for a surgery, the whole production line would grind to a halt. 

So no, absolutely no surgeries. No procedures. I haven't been cut open, I haven't been stitched up. I am one hundred percent original, factory-installed parts, and they are all running perfectly! Better than perfectly! I'm telling you, I don't need doctors, I don't need procedures, I just need people to keep up with me!
Has anyone told you that your ideas about your abilities or plans seem unrealistic or impossible?

Unrealistic? Impossible? Ha! Doc, that's just the sound of people who can't keep up! Nobody outright tells me my ideas are impossible, but you should see the looks I get. It's like they're looking at a UFO or something. I'll be down at the plant, right? And I'll tell the foreman, I'll say, "Look, if we recalibrate the primary crusher to a slightly wider gauge and run the secondary grinders at a twenty percent faster clip, we can increase output by a third before lunch!" 

And what do they do? They just blink at me. Just... blink. Like I'm speaking Greek! They don't say it's impossible, they just say, "Whoa there, slow down, we have protocols." Protocols! That's just a fancy word for being lazy, if you ask me. 

And Martha, my wife, she's the same way. The other night, I was up late—because who needs sleep when your brain is firing like a V8 engine, right?—and I drafted up this whole plan to reorganize our entire garage. I'm talking custom shelving, a whole new pegboard system for my tools, color-coded bins for the hardware. I even drew up a schematic for running new electrical lines so I can set up a heavy-duty air compressor right there next to the workbench. I showed it to her at breakfast, and she just sighed. She didn't say it was impossible, she just said, "Can't you just sit still and drink your coffee?" 

Sit still! Why would I sit still when I have the energy to completely revolutionize our storage space before noon? People just don't get it, Doc. They're so used to moving at a snail's pace, dragging themselves through the day, that when they see somebody operating at maximum efficiency, they think it's crazy. But it's not crazy, it's vision! It's ambition! They don't tell me I'm unrealistic, they just... they just get out of my way because they know they can't stop me! So no, nobody's told me my plans are impossible. They just don't have the horsepower to understand them!
Have you recently taken prednisone or any other steroid medicine?

Steroids? Prednisone? Doc, I feel like a broken record here. No! No steroids, no pills, no injections, nothing! 

Why on earth would I need steroids? Aren't those the things bodybuilders take to get all puffed up? Or what they give you when you have a terrible rash from poison ivy? Because let me tell you, I haven't been anywhere near poison ivy. I don't even have time to go into the woods! Who has time for hiking when there's so much to do? And as for bodybuilding, well, hauling fifty-pound bags of cement mix and wrestling with the hopper controls all day down at the plant keeps me in plenty good shape. Look at these arms! Solid rock, Doc. I don't need any artificial enhancements.

I remember my buddy Frank, he took prednisone once. This was years ago, back when we were still running the old rotary crushers before they upgraded the whole system. Frank got this awful allergic reaction to some kind of solvent they were testing out for cleaning the gears. His face swelled up like a balloon, I mean, he looked like a tomato with eyes. They put him on prednisone, and he was miserable! Said it made him feel jittery, couldn't sleep, he was sweating all the time. 

Now, I know what you're thinking. You're thinking, "Aha! He's jittery and not sleeping, maybe he's on steroids!" But that's where you're wrong, Doc! See, Frank was miserable because it was unnatural for him. He was a low-energy guy to begin with. Me? I'm naturally high-octane! I don't need a pill to make me feel this good. This is all me! This is pure, unadulterated, one hundred percent natural energy flowing through my veins! 

So no, I haven't taken any prednisone. I haven't taken any steroids. I don't even take aspirin for a headache, mostly because I don't get headaches anymore! My head is clear as a bell! I am running on all cylinders, naturally, without any chemical help whatsoever!
Has your wife or daughter said you seem physically different or medically unwell lately?

Physically different? Medically unwell? No, no, I mean, why would they say that? If anything, they think I look too good! Martha hasn't said a single word about me looking sick. Not one. Mostly she just tells me I need to, you know, act my age. Act my age! I'm seventy-four years old, Doc, but my engine is running like I'm twenty-five! 

And my daughter... well, she came by the house on Sunday. Usually, she just brings the kids over and sits on the patio, maybe drinks some iced tea, but this past weekend I was already up on the roof. I decided the gutters needed a complete overhaul, not just a cleaning, but realigning the pitch so the runoff flows better toward the downspouts. It's a simple physics problem, really, just adjusting the brackets. Anyway, she pulls into the driveway, gets out of her car, and she doesn't look up at me and say, "Oh, Dad, you look medically unwell." No! She yells, "Dad, get down from there before you break a hip!" 

Break a hip! Can you believe the nerve? I've got the balance of a mountain goat up there! I was up and down that aluminum extension ladder maybe... gosh, maybe fifteen times before she even showed up. I wasn't even breathing hard! So no, they don't think I'm sick. They just... they just worry because they can't fathom a man my age having this kind of stamina. They think because I've got some miles on the odometer I should be parked in a recliner watching golf tournaments all afternoon. 

But I'm not sick! I'm the absolute opposite of sick! I look in the mirror these days and I swear to you, I look ten years younger. I've got color in my cheeks, my eyes are bright, I am vibrant! If I were medically unwell, do you honestly think I could be running the primary crushers and the blending hoppers down at the plant the way I do? Of course not. So no, they haven't said I look unwell. They just complain that I won't sit still and rest. But like I keep telling them, rest is for the weary, and I have never been less weary in my entire life!

So, no, trouble with my memory? Absolutely not. If anything, I'm remembering things I hadn't thought about in years, and I'm connecting the dots faster than anyone else around me. Hearing or seeing things? Like... hallucinations? No, no, I haven't got anything like that going on. I know my mind is racing a mile a minute, but my eyes and ears are working exactly the same as they always have. 

Well, I mean, I see things other people don't see, but not in the way you mean. Not ghosts or visions or anything crazy like that. I see things because I'm actually paying attention. Like down at the plant, I can see the exact moment the mixture starts to clump in the hopper—the younger guys, they just stare at their phones, but I can see the texture changing, I can hear the pitch of the motor whining just a fraction of a decibel higher when the load gets too heavy. I see the structural flaws, I hear the engine strain, I notice when the church bulletin has a typo in the second paragraph. But as for hearing voices or seeing things that aren't physically there? Absolutely not. My mind is sharp, Doc, it's not playing tricks on me. It's just working better than everyone else's right now.

A change? Well, I suppose you could call it a change, but I prefer to think of it as an awakening, really. You see, for the last few years, especially since I hit my seventies, people just expect you to slow down. My wife would say, "Frank, you're always tired," and I'd say, "I've been mixing concrete and crushing aggregate for four decades, of course I'm tired." 

But this? This is entirely different. It's not just a change, it's a complete reversal! I feel like I did back in 1982 when we got the contract for the new municipal building and I was working sixty-hour weeks and still had the energy to build that deck on the back of our first house on Elm Street. Like I was just saying, I was tired. But there is a world of difference between being tired from working a physically demanding job and being depressed. Nice people, the Johnsons. They ended up moving to Boca Raton back in '94, I think it was, or maybe '95. Anyway, I was working essentially three jobs to save up for a better house for the family. So I was driven, sure. I had a goal, I had ambition. 

But was I energized like this? No. Absolutely not. Back then, I was running on sheer willpower and maybe a little too much cheap diner coffee. I was dragging myself out of bed every morning. I'd get home and my work boots would feel like they were made of solid lead. I was productive, but I was exhausted. 

This thing happening right now, this... this absolute surge? It's completely unprecedented. I have never felt anything even close to this in my entire seventy-four years on this earth. Even when I was eighteen and thought I could conquer the world, I still needed to sleep! I still got tired after a long day of hauling materials. But now? I don't feel the fatigue. I don't feel the drag. It's like my body just bypassed the need for all that. 

So, no, Doc, I can confidently say I have never, ever experienced a time like this before. Never. This is a brand new chapter, and let me tell you, it's the best one yet. I mean, if I had felt like this in my thirties, I would own the plant by now! I would be running the whole tri-state operation! I haven't started any new medications because I don't even take any old ones. Like I said, my health is perfect. Better than perfect. 

And substances? If you mean drugs or... or whatever, well, I should hope you know better than to ask a man like me that. I've been working at the same plant since Jimmy Carter was in office! We get drug tested randomly, you know. Strict OSHA regulations. Safety first, always. You absolutely cannot be operating a three-ton industrial mixer, calibrating the aggregate flow, if you're hopped up on... whatever it is the kids are taking these days. You'd lose an arm, or worse, you'd ruin a fifty-thousand-dollar batch of concrete! 

And even the legal stuff, the over-the-counter junk? I don't touch it. I see these young guys on the floor, they come in at 6 AM for the early shift clutching these giant cans of energy drinks. Neon green cans, looks like actual antifreeze, smells like bubblegum and battery acid. They chug those things just to keep their eyes open! It's pathetic, really. I tell them, "You're rotting your stomach lining! You're gonna have an ulcer by the time you're thirty!" But they don't listen. Me? I drink my black coffee at 4:30 in the morning, made in my regular drip pot, and that is it. I don't need pills, I don't need powders, I don't need vitamins, and I certainly don't need neon energy drinks. 

So no, I haven't started taking anything at all. Nothing. This energy you're seeing right now? This drive to just get up and conquer the day? It's one hundred percent pure, unadulterated Frank. Just natural, God-given vitality that's finally been completely unleashed. Why in the world would I mess a good thing up by putting chemicals in my body?
